summary: The article provides largely accurate information regarding tax-saving avenues under the new tax regime for AY 2026-27, but contains a few inaccuracies regarding the standard deduction limit and employer NPS contribution limits for the new tax regime.

claims.claim: Salaried individuals can still claim a Standard Deduction of ₹50,000 under the new regime from AY 2024-25 onwards.
claims.note: For the new tax regime, the standard deduction for salaried individuals was increased to ₹75,000 from AY 2024-25 onwards, not ₹50,000.

claims.claim: For salaried employees, this deduction [employer's contribution to NPS under Section 80CCD(2)] is capped at 10% of their basic salary plus Dearness Allowance (DA). For Central Government employees, this limit is 14%.
claims.note: Under the new tax regime, the employer's contribution to NPS under Section 80CCD(2) is deductible up to 14% of salary for all employees, not just Central Government employees. For the old tax regime, it is 10%.

claims.claim: Donations to specified funds and institutions under Section 80G can provide tax relief, subject to certain limits.
claims.note: Deductions under Section 80G are generally not allowed under the new tax regime.

claims.claim: Donations can be made to government-established funds, approved charitable institutions, or even certain political parties (under Section 80GGC, though this is separate from 80G).
claims.note: Donations to certain funds and institutions are eligible for deduction under Section 80G, and donations to political parties are covered under Section 80GGC.

claims.claim: For cash donations exceeding ₹2,000, no deduction is allowed.
claims.note: Cash donations exceeding ₹2,000 are not eligible for deduction under Section 80G.

claims.claim: if you have a home loan for a property that is *let out* (rented out), you can still claim a deduction for the interest paid on that loan under Section 24(b) of the Income Tax Act.
claims.note: Interest paid on a home loan for a let-out property is deductible under Section 24(b) in both old and new tax regimes.

claims.claim: the maximum amount of gratuity exempt from tax for non-government employees is ₹20 lakhs (for those covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972) or ₹20 lakhs (for those not covered), subject to specific calculations.
claims.note: The maximum gratuity exemption for non-government employees is ₹20 lakhs, whether covered by the Payment of Gratuity Act or not, subject to other conditions.

claims.claim: leave encashment on retirement can be exempt up to ₹25 lakhs for non-government employees, subject to certain conditions.
claims.note: The exemption limit for leave encashment for non-government employees on retirement was increased to ₹25 lakhs from April 1, 2023.

claims.claim: Compensation received under a Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS) can also be exempt from tax, up to a limit of ₹5 lakhs, provided certain conditions laid out in Section 10(10C) of the Income Tax Act are met.
claims.note: Compensation received under VRS is exempt up to ₹5 lakhs under Section 10(10C), subject to conditions.

claims.claim: For individuals who are part of the Agnipath scheme, contributions made to the Agniveer Corpus Fund are eligible for deduction under Section 80CCH. Both the individual's contribution and the matching contribution by the Central Government to the Agniveer Corpus Fund are deductible from taxable income.
claims.note: Under the new tax regime, only the Central Government's contribution to the Agniveer Corpus Fund is deductible under Section 80CCH. The individual's own contribution is deductible only under the old tax regime.

article_title: New Tax Regime: 5 Ways to Reduce Your Tax for AY 2026-27
